articles.summary: Vicki Seppala Retires After Three Decades with Freeport mboyle Thu, 07/16/2026 - 13:48 Post Image July 16, 2026 - Email was the hot new technology when Vicki Seppala first got into the mining business more than three decades ago. Seppala had been working at a technology startup before joining Freeport, so she knew email – like any emerging technology – would create both opportunities and challenges. Email allowed instant and widespread communication. It also gobbled up a lot of time. That lesson stayed with her throughout her career. As a trailblazer who became the first woman mine manager in Chile, Seppala learned that progress often brings both benefits and challenges. Whether evaluating new technologies, managing complex projects or planning for future growth, those experiences proved valuable as she and her team worked to plan the future expansion of the Safford mine and its vast Lone Star reserves. Seppala retired recently as General Manager at Safford, closing a mining career that began in 1995 and took her from an entry-level geological engineer to leadership roles at mine sites across North and South America. Designing the future at Safford As Seppala’s retirement at the end of June neared, her focus was less on herself and more on industry advancements and the outlook for the site where she spent the previous four years. Safford is Freeport’s newest mine in the United States and has the potential to become one of its top producers, with estimates that future expansions could deliver an additional 300 to 400 million pounds of copper per year by the 2030s. It could be in operation for 100 years or more, Seppala said. Helping plan a project of that magnitude and length means predicting what mining will look like decades from now and integrating emerging technology still being developed. It also means working closely with a vast team of technical experts that Seppala credits with “doing the heavy lifting.” The mining industry in general and Freeport in particular have embraced high-tech solutions to squeeze more copper and other metals from the same ore bodies. Like email, that creates new opportunities and challenges. “Trying to understand how to take advantage of the technology that we have when it’s changing so rapidly complicates things a bit,” Seppala said. “It’s exciting and exhilarating to think about how different the Safford mine might look because we have the opportunity to really try to understand the direction that all of these technologies are going and build Safford in a way that can more readily take advantage of those things. It’s liberating because there are so many possibilities. But it’s also very difficult to draw the line in the sand.” Connections to the community Outside of work, Seppala, who graduated from the University of Arizona with a bachelor’s degree in Geological Engineering, has enjoyed time with family and participating in various outdoor activities – hiking, bicycling, camping and wildlife. She also has been active in various civic organizations, including the Lowell Institute for Mineral Resources at the University of Arizona; the Society for Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration; and Women in Mining, where she has served as an advocate and mentor for women pursuing mining careers. “We all live in these communities in which we work,” she said. “We all want to be proud of what we do and make sure that we do what’s right.” One of Seppala’s career highlights is being part of an industry shift that has seen women become a much larger share of the workforce at all levels. A trailblazer herself, Seppala became Chile’s first woman mine manager in 2006 and later served as mine manager at Morenci and general manager of the Climax and Safford mines. Retiring now comes with mixed emotions as this is such a historic time for mining, Seppala said shortly before her last day at Freeport at the end of June. “We are in the middle of writing a very exciting chapter about the dynamic change of mining right now,” she said. “People are going to write books about it in the future, and our company is at the forefront of the innovations in copper processing. It’s going to explode into something that’s game changing in the industry.” Photo: Vicki Seppala was the first woman mine manager in Chile in 2006 and has held other top management positions with Freeport.
articles.title: Vicki Seppala Retires After Three Decades with Freeport

articles.summary: You're committed to making healthy changes to yourself. You started a GLP-1 medication, your appetite changed, the weight began to move, but then a few months later, your hair starts showing up everywhere: in the shower, in your brush, and on your pillow. That kind of shedding can feel personal, especially when you are doing something positive for your health. So it is natural to ask: do GLP-1 medications cause hair loss? The good news is that current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly damage hair follicles. Instead, rapid weight loss, lower food intake, and nutrient changes can place stress on the body, which may push more hairs into the resting phase. Doctors often evaluate this kind of diffuse shedding as possible telogen effluvium, a common and usually temporary type of shedding that can happen after major changes like weight loss, illness, surgery, stress, or hormonal changes. This kind of shedding is often a sign that your body and scalp need support, not a sign that your hair is gone for good. GLP-1 Hair Loss Is Usually Linked to Weight Loss, Not Follicle Damage GLP-1 medications are used to support blood sugar management, weight management, and certain cardiometabolic health goals, depending on the specific prescription and patient need. Hair loss is not commonly framed as direct follicle damage in this context, although some patients still report shedding during a GLP-1 routine. That can feel confusing. Your experience can still be real even when hair loss is not considered a common listed side effect for every GLP-1 medication. More likely, the link between GLP-1 medications and hair shedding is indirect. When someone eats less, loses weight quickly, or gets less protein and key nutrients during treatment, the body may respond to that change as stress. More hairs can move into the resting phase, and a few months later, those resting hairs may shed at the same time. GLP-1 Medications Do Not Appear to Attack Hair Follicles Directly Current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly damage the follicle. In many cases, the follicle is still active beneath the surface. It may simply be resting. That's important because resting follicles can often return to the growth phase once the body stabilizes. Most GLP-1-Related Shedding Is Temporary Hair shedding can feel alarming, but it does not automatically mean permanent hair loss. Many cases that fit telogen effluvium improve once the trigger settles and the body receives consistent support. Talk with your prescribing clinician before changing any GLP-1 medication. Then review your nutrition, watch for other symptoms, and support your scalp with a gentle, consistent routine. How Weight Loss on GLP-1 Medications Can Affect the Hair Cycle Hair follicles are sensitive to change. They rely on steady nutrition, energy, and internal balance to keep producing strong, healthy-looking strands. Telogen effluvium happens when more hairs than usual move into the resting phase of the hair cycle. This can happen after weight loss, illness, surgery, stress, hormonal changes, medication changes, or a major diet change. With GLP-1 medications, the trigger may be the change happening around treatment: less food, faster weight loss, and lower intake of nutrients that help support normal hair growth. Here is the simple version: Appetite drops or weight changes quickly. The body experiences internal stress. More follicles move into the resting phase. Two to four months later, those resting hairs shed together. Lower Appetite Can Mean Lower Hair-Supportive Nutrition Many people eat less during GLP-1-supported weight loss, especially when fullness comes sooner or meals become smaller. When food intake drops sharply, protein and micronutrient intake may drop too. Hair production is an active biological process. Your follicles need consistent support from nutrients like protein, iron, B vitamins, vitamin D, and zinc. Nutrient gaps do not cause every case of hair loss, but low protein intake, low iron stores, and certain vitamin or mineral deficiencies may contribute to shedding for some people. GLP-1 Hair Loss Often Shows Up Months Later One of the most confusing parts of GLP-1-related hair loss is the timing. You may feel fine at first. Your appetite changes. Your weight begins to move. Then, a few months later, the hair shedding becomes hard to miss. Some people may also notice a wider-looking part line or more visible thinning around the crown, especially in certain lighting. Signs Your Shedding May Fit Telogen Effluvium Shedding started 2 to 4 months after weight loss or appetite change. Hair falls from across the scalp rather than one patch. More strands appear in the shower, brush, or pillow. The scalp does not show scarring, pain, or severe inflammation. The part line or ponytail looks thinner than usual. If this sounds familiar, try not to panic. Look at the full picture: how quickly your weight changed, whether your protein intake dropped, whether nutrient levels may be low, and whether stress, styling habits, or hormonal changes may also be contributing. Your hair may be responding to a season of change. With the right support, your body and scalp can have a steadier foundation while the hair cycle recovers. A steady plan can support your body, protect your scalp, and give fragile hair the gentler care it needs while the hair cycle resets. articles.summary: Have you noticed more hair on your hair brush or in the drain after you shower? If you're taking a GLP-1 medication, it may not be just in your head. You may be shedding more hair than usual. Hair shedding during weight loss does not always mean something is wrong with your hair. Your body may simply be adapting while your meals have become smaller. Hair is sensitive to overall nourishment. When appetite drops, certain nutrients can become easier to miss, even when you are still making healthy choices. How Reduced Appetite Can Leave Hair-Supporting Nutrients Behind GLP-1 medications can help you feel full sooner, which often means you eat less throughout the day. For your hair, a smaller appetite becomes important when smaller meals no longer provide enough protein, iron, zinc, B vitamins, vitamin D, and other nutrients your body uses to support healthy hair. Hair shedding has been reported during GLP-1 treatment, but the connection is often tied to weight change, lower intake, or other body stressors rather than the medication directly attacking hair. Your body is smart about priorities. During rapid weight loss, lower intake, nausea, or skipped meals, it may direct energy and nutrients toward the functions it needs most. Hair may be one place where that change becomes noticeable because follicles are sensitive to nutrition, stress, and the body's daily rhythm. Targeted supplements may be helpful when food intake or bloodwork points to a real nutrient gap. A better starting point is understanding what your hair may be missing, what your body may need, and how to support both your nutrition and scalp with consistency. Smaller Meals Can Still Miss Key Nutrients Healthy choices can still fall short when portions become much smaller. You may be eating cleaner, lighter, or more intentionally, while your total nutrient intake still drops. A fruit breakfast may feel refreshing, but it may not give your body enough protein. A small salad may feel balanced, but it may not provide enough iron, zinc, B12, or vitamin D. During a GLP-1 routine, steady nutrient coverage matters more than perfect eating. Food, testing, and clinician guidance help you understand your internal nutrient needs. A scalp-first routine helps care for the outside foundation, especially when shedding has made your hair feel more fragile or your scalp needs extra attention. When your appetite gets smaller on a GLP-1 medication, protein can become harder to get enough of. It may also be one of the first things to fall off the plate because protein-rich foods often feel more filling than fruit, crackers, soup, or lighter meals. When intake stays too low, your body may have less support available for non-essential tissues like hair. Protein deficiency hair loss can happen during periods of rapid weight loss or reduced intake. You do not need to eat perfectly. When you know you may not finish a full plate, eat the protein portion first, then move to the rest of the meal. Simple protein-first ideas include: Eggs before toast Greek yogurt before fruit Chicken, fish, tofu, or lean meat before rice or pasta Cottage cheese or a protein smoothie when a full meal feels difficult Lentils, beans, or tempeh for plant-forward meals Protein first does not mean protein only. It simply gives your hair and body the raw materials they need before fullness sets in. 02 Iron Helps Hair Follicles Get the Oxygen They Need Iron plays a subtle but important role in hair health. It helps red blood cells move oxygen through the body, including to the active tissues that support the hair cycle. When iron stores run low, follicles may not get the same steady support they need to stay in rhythm. Ferritin is the storage form of iron, and it often comes up when shedding becomes noticeable. You can have low iron stores before obvious anemia shows up, which is why ferritin testing can be helpful for some people. This may be worth discussing if you have heavy periods, eat little or no meat, follow a vegetarian or vegan diet, or find yourself eating much smaller meals on a GLP-1 routine. Ask About Ferritin Before Guessing With Iron Hair shedding alone cannot tell you whether your iron is low. Lean red meat Poultry Seafood Lentils Beans Spinach Pumpkin seeds Iron-fortified cereals Plant-based iron sources pair well with vitamin C foods like citrus, strawberries, bell peppers, tomatoes, or broccoli. Oysters & shellfish Beef Turkey Pumpkin seeds Chickpeas Lentils Cashews Yogurt Small additions can build over time. articles.summary: Employee Management Payroll Data Management for HR Professionals: Best Practices for Accuracy and Compliance Oluwakemi Adesina July 16, 2026 Payroll data management for HR professionals is the practice of keeping every piece of employee pay information (salaries, bank details, tax records, pension contributions) organised, accurate, and easy to retrieve. It’s less exciting than most HR tasks, and that’s why it matters: when done well, it doesn’t have to be repeated. This guide covers how to structure payroll records, keep them accurate, and stay compliant without making payroll a monthly fire drill. What Is Payroll Data Management for HR Professionals? Payroll data management is the practice of collecting, organising, storing, and maintaining all information required to pay employees accurately and legally. That includes salary structures, bank details, tax identification numbers, pension records, leave balances, and every document tied to a person’s employment history. Employee payroll data typically falls into a few categories: personal identification (names, tax IDs, bank accounts), compensation details (salary, bonuses, deductions), statutory records (pension, tax, NHF contributions), and historical records (payslips, appraisals, contract changes). HR payroll records must be structured so anyone on the team can find what they need. Businesses need structured records for a simple reason: payroll touches law, money, and people simultaneously. Getting it right, and payroll becomes another easy operational process: accurate, on time, and easy to account for. Common Payroll Data Challenges Duplicate Record: When an employee gets entered twice after a department transfer, creating two payslips for the same person in the same month. Manual Entry Errors: A salary typed with an extra zero, a pension percentage copied from the wrong column, a bank account number transposed by one digit. Missing Employee Information: A new hire whose tax ID hasn’t been captured, or a departed employee whose final pay is delayed because bank details weren’t updated. Data inconsistencies: such as the same employee listed with two job titles across systems, slow down audits and reporting. When HR payroll records are stored in three places instead of one, these inconsistencies multiply quickly. Best Practices for Payroll Data Management for HR Professionals Good payroll records management starts with standardization. Every employee record should follow the same format, fields, and naming conventions so nothing depends on one person remembering how it was set up. A few practices consistently prevent the problems above: Standardized record templates for every employee, updated the same way every time Regular data updates whenever a salary, bank detail, or statutory status changes Secure storage for confidential employee information, with backups not just on a single laptop Access controls so only the people who need it can view employee payroll data Data validation checks before payroll runs, catching errors before they become payments Payroll Data Security and Compliance Payroll data is among the most sensitive information a business holds: bank details, tax IDs, salary figures, and addresses. Protecting it is an HR compliance responsibility. Strong payroll data security is more about discipline: who has access, why they have it, and how quickly that access can be revoked when it’s no longer needed. Payroll compliance records must be retained for a defined period, organised to be produced on request, and secured against unauthorized access. Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act, businesses processing personal data, including payroll data, have legal obligations regarding data storage, access, and breach handling. It’s worth reviewing current requirements with the NDPC, as the framework has evolved from older NITDA-era rules many businesses still assume apply. Audit readiness follows the same logic as good documentation: if a regulator or auditor asked for payroll records tomorrow, could the business produce them within a day? Centralised payroll documentation makes that answer “yes” instead of “give us a week.” How Technology Improves Payroll Data Management A centralized database makes this better. Instead of employee information scattered across spreadsheets, email attachments, and personal drives, every record lives in one place, in one format, and updated once. Automated updates eliminate the most common source of manual-entry errors. When a salary changes or an employee’s bank details are updated, the system shows the change everywhere at once. Reporting dashboards turn what used to be a multi-day exercise into something that takes minutes: pull the report, filter by department or date range, and done! Workflow automation connects it all together, routing approvals, updates, and payroll runs through a consistent process rather than a chain of emails and reminders. Improving Payroll Records Management with Eazipay Eazipay centralizes payroll records with payroll compliance built in to understand Nigerian regulatory system. Every employee’s payroll documentation (salary history, statutory deductions, payslips, bank details) are stored in a single system. Combined with payroll reporting that’s ready on demand and secure administration that controls who can access confidential employee data, Eazipay gives HR teams the kind of compliance visibility that used to take a dedicated audit to assemble. If you’d like to see how it fits your team, you can get in touch here. FAQs What is payroll data management? Payroll data management is the practice of collecting, organizing, and preserving employee payroll information: salaries, deductions, bank details, and statutory records, accurately and securely. Why is payroll data important? Because errors in payroll data lead directly to compliance breaches, incorrect payments, and disputes with employees, problems that are far more expensive to fix after the fact than to prevent upfront. How long should payroll records be kept? Retention periods vary by record type and applicable regulations, so businesses should confirm current requirements with bodies such as the NRS and PenCom rather than relying on general assumptions. How can businesses improve payroll data accuracy? Standardize record formats, validate data before every payroll run, restrict access to sensitive fields, and update records as changes happen rather than in periodic batches. What payroll software features help manage employee records? Centralized databases, automated updates, access controls, audit-ready reporting dashboards, and secure storage are the features that matter most for accurate, compliant payroll records management.
